claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange that seeks to address concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of selected experiments from a number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (RP:CB) is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange that seeks to address concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of selected experiments from a number of high-profile papers in the field of cancer biology (Errington et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Errington et al., 2014, which describes the project.

claim: For each paper in the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, a Registered Report detailing the proposed experimental designs and protocols for the replications was peer reviewed and published prior to data collection.
source: For each of these papers a Registered Report detailing the proposed experimental designs and protocols for the replications was peer reviewed and published prior to data collection.
evidence: This claim describes the methodology of the RP:CB project and is supported by the citation to the Registered Report (Eaton et al., 2015).

claim: In 2012, Arthur et al. reported results that intestinal inflammation modifies the gut microbiota affecting the progression of colorectal cancer.
source: In 2012, Arthur et al. reported results that intestinal inflammation modifies the gut microbiota affecting the progression of colorectal cancer (CRC).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from the original Arthur et al. 2012 study.

claim: The model used by Arthur et al. was a combination of interleukin-10-deficient (Il10-/-) mice and E. coli mono-association to produce a background of chronic inflammation followed by six weekly injections of AOM to induce neoplastic transformation.
source: The model used by Arthur and colleagues was a combination of interleukin-10-deficient (Il10-/- ) mice and E. coli mono-association to produce a background of chronic inflammation followed by six weekly injections of AOM to induce neoplastic transformation.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental model used in the original study.

claim: Germ-free mice mono-associated with the commensal mouse adherent-invasive E. coli strain NC101 developed invasive mucinous carcinomas which did not occur in mice mono-associated with Enterococcus faecalis.
source: Using this inflammation-induced CRC model, Arthur and colleagues reported that germ-free mice mono-associated with the commensal mouse adherent-invasive E. coli strain NC101 developed invasive mucinous carcinomas which did not occur in mice mono-associated with Enterococcus faecalis, another colitis-inducing bacterial strain (Arthur et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the original Arthur et al. 2012 study.

claim: NC101 harbors the polyketide synthase (pks) pathogenicity island that encodes the biosynthetic machinery for synthesizing the genotoxin colibactin.
source: NC101 harbors the polyketide synthase (pks) pathogenicity island that encodes the biosynthetic machinery for synthesizing the genotoxin colibactin (Nougayrède et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nougayrède et al., 2006.

claim: Similar observations to Arthur et al. 2012 were observed using APCMin/+ mice.
source: Similar observations were observed using APCMin/+ mice (Bonnet et al., 2014), germ-free APCMin/+; Il10-/- mice (Tomkovich et al., 2017), or a AOM-DDS xenograft mouse model of CRC (Cougnoux et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bonnet et al., 2014.

claim: Similar observations to Arthur et al. 2012 were observed using germ-free APCMin/+; Il10-/- mice.
source: Similar observations were observed using APCMin/+ mice (Bonnet et al., 2014), germ-free APCMin/+; Il10-/- mice (Tomkovich et al., 2017), or a AOM-DDS xenograft mouse model of CRC (Cougnoux et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tomkovich et al., 2017.

claim: Similar observations to Arthur et al. 2012 were observed using an AOM-DDS xenograft mouse model of CRC.
source: Similar observations were observed using APCMin/+ mice (Bonnet et al., 2014), germ-free APCMin/+; Il10-/- mice (Tomkovich et al., 2017), or a AOM-DDS xenograft mouse model of CRC (Cougnoux et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cougnoux et al., 2014.

claim: A follow-up study by Arthur and colleagues reported that colonic inflammation was necessary for the tumor-promoting activity of NC101 through modulation of specific microbial genes.
source: A follow-up study by Arthur and colleagues, reported that colonic inflammation was necessary for the tumor-promoting activity of NC101 through modulation of specific microbial genes (Arthur et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arthur et al., 2014.

claim: Most mice did not survive to the planned 18-week post-AOM time point, and either died or were euthanized prior to the intended study end-point.
source: In this study, we found most mice did not survive to the planned 18-week post-AOM time point, and either died or were euthanized prior to the intended study end-point (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: There were similar levels of colonization capacity in vivo for both NC101 and NC101Δpks strains of bacteria.
source: Importantly, there were similar levels of colonization capacity in vivo for both strains of bacteria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), similar to the original study, suggesting bacterial load was not a factor in the survival differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bacterial load was not a factor in the survival differences between NC101 and NC101Δpks mono-associated mice.
source: Importantly, there were similar levels of colonization capacity in vivo for both strains of bacteria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), similar to the original study, suggesting bacterial load was not a factor in the survival differences.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of similar colonization levels between the two bacterial strains.

claim: An exploratory analysis comparing the survival distributions between NC101 and NC101Δpks groups during the 18-week timeframe was statistically significant (log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test; p = 0.0230).
source: An exploratory analysis to compare the survival distributions between the two groups during this timeframe was statistically significant (log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test; p = 0.0230).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of survival data.

claim: Early death that occurred during AOM treatment was associated with widespread liver lesions.
source: During this study, early death that occurred during AOM treatment was associated with widespread liver lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological observations.

claim: Mice that died during AOM treatment had liver lesions of less severity, including widespread hepatocellular vacuolation and multifocal hepatocellular necrosis.
source: The other mice that died during AOM treatment had liver lesions of less severity, including widespread hepatocellular vacuolation and multifocal hepatocellular necrosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mice that died after the AOM treatment phase all had chronic liver lesions suggestive of a regenerative response to ongoing damage.
source: Mice that died after the AOM treatment phase all had chronic liver lesions suggestive of a regenerative response to ongoing damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological observations.

claim: There was no evidence of fibrosis even in the most chronic liver lesions.
source: Surprisingly, there was no evidence of fibrosis even in the most chronic lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological observations.

claim: Colitis first appeared at the start of AOM treatment (5 weeks after mono-association) and was present in all mice that were examined histologically 9 weeks or more after mono-association.
source: In the mice that died or were euthanized prematurely, colitis first appeared at the start of AOM treatment (5 weeks after mono-association) and was present in all mice that were examined histologically 9 weeks or more after mono-association.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological observations.

claim: Most mice also had typhlitis, which was less severe than the colitis.
source: Most mice also had typhlitis, which was less severe than the colitis.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological observations.

claim: Colon adenocarcinoma was first detected in mice that died 8 weeks after AOM treatment (17 weeks after mono-association) and was present in all mice euthanized 13 weeks or more after AOM treatment.
source: Colon adenocarcinoma was first detected in mice that died 8 weeks after AOM treatment (17 weeks after mono-association) and was present in all mice euthanized 13 weeks or more after AOM treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological observations.

claim: The severity of chronic lesions and extent of neoplasia were greater in this replication attempt than what was reported in the original study.
source: In addition to the increased early death rate during and immediately after AOM treatment in this replication attempt, severity of chronic lesions and extent of neoplasia were greater than what was reported in the original study.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of histopathological observations between the replication and original study.

claim: The increased severity of lesions in the replication attempt is most likely due to the longer experimental timing that occurred compared to the original study.
source: This is most likely due to the longer experimental timing that occurred in this replication attempted compared to the original study.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the difference in experimental timing between studies.

claim: Lesions were similar in morphology to those described in the original study, but more severe.
source: Lesions were similar in morphology to those described in the original study, but more severe.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of histopathological observations between the replication and original study.

claim: Grossly evident colon thickening was present in mice examined 22 or more weeks after mono-associations.
source: Grossly evident colon thickening was present in mice examined 22 or more weeks after mono-associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by gross pathological observations.

claim: Individual tumors could not be distinguished either grossly or histologically in the most severely affected mice.
source: These lesions were widespread and coalescing, and unlike in the original study, individual masses could not be distinguished either grossly or histologically (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gross and histopathological observations presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When considering all the mice that survived 14 weeks post-AOM treatment or later, the median scores for inflammation, invasion, and neoplasia were at or near the maximum possible for both NC101 and NC101Δpks cohorts.
source: When considering all the mice that survived 14 weeks post-AOM treatment (5 weeks beyond the endpoint in Arthur et al., 2012), or later, the median scores for each measure were at or near the maximum possible for both cohorts (inflammation = 6; invasion = 8; neoplasia = 5) (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histopathological scoring data presented in Figure 3B–D.

claim: The difference in severity of inflammation, invasion, and neoplasia between the two studies are most likely explained by the increased experimental timing that occurred in this replication attempt that differed from the original study.
source: As noted above, the difference in severity of inflammation, invasion, and neoplasia between the two studies are most likely explained by the increased experimental timing that occurred in this replication attempt that differed from the original study.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the difference in experimental timing between studies.

claim: The absolute scores for inflammation and invasion were greater in this replication attempt compared to the original study.
source: The absolute scores were greater in this replication attempt compared to the original study, particularly for inflammation and invasion, which, combined with the survival and histopathological observations described above suggests that lesions were more severe and/or progressive over time in this replication attempt than in the original study.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of histopathological scoring data between the replication and original study.

claim: Lesions were more severe and/or progressive over time in this replication attempt than in the original study.
source: The absolute scores were greater in this replication attempt compared to the original study, particularly for inflammation and invasion, which, combined with the survival and histopathological observations described above suggests that lesions were more severe and/or progressive over time in this replication attempt than in the original study.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of histopathological data and survival observations.

claim: Any differences attributable to the absence of pks would have been masked by the greatly increased severity of the lesions.
source: Any differences attributable to the absence of pks would have been masked by the greatly increased severity of the lesions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the severity of lesions observed.

claim: Over time it is possible the products of excessive inflammatory responses (e.g. reactive oxygen species), which promote tumorigenesis, become more important than pks status.
source: Additionally, over time it is possible the products of excessive inflammatory responses (e.g. reactive oxygen species), which promote tumorigenesis, become more important than pks status.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the role of inflammatory products over time.

claim: A meta-analysis of survival effects resulted in a HR of 1.92, 95% CI [1.11, 3.30], which was statistically significant (p = 0.0188).
source: A meta-analysis (Figure 4) of these effects resulted in a HR of 1.92, 95% CI [1.11, 3.30], which was statistically significant (p = 0.0188) and implies the null hypothesis that the survival distributions for the two cohorts are the same, can be rejected.
evidence: This claim is supported by meta-analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The meta-analysis implies the null hypothesis that the survival distributions for the two cohorts are the same can be rejected.
source: A meta-analysis (Figure 4) of these effects resulted in a HR of 1.92, 95% CI [1.11, 3.30], which was statistically significant (p = 0.0188) and implies the null hypothesis that the survival distributions for the two cohorts are the same, can be rejected.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the statistically significant meta-analysis result.

claim: The experimental timing used in this replication attempt was different from the original study, which evaluated colonic inflammation and tumorigenesis 18 weeks after mono-association rather than 18 weeks after AOM treatment.
source: During peer review of this Replication Study, however, one of the reviewers suggested that the experimental timing used in this replication attempt was different from the original study, which evaluated colonic inflammation and tumorigenesis 18 weeks after mono-association rather than 18 weeks after AOM treatment as was described in the Registered Report and performed in this study.
evidence: This claim is based on feedback received during peer review.

claim: This replication attempt had an experimental endpoint 9 weeks longer than the original study.
source: Thus, this replication attempt had an experimental endpoint 9 weeks longer than the original study.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the difference in experimental timing between studies.

claim: This methodological error was based on the methods derived from the original study and not corrected on review of the Registered Report.
source: This methodological error, which confounds the interpretation of the results of this replication attempt, was based on the methods derived from the original study and not corrected on review of the Registered Report (Eaton et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on the history of the experimental design and review process.

claim: Germ-free mice differ from conventional mice in that they do not normally develop colitis, even in the absence of IL-10.
source: First, the model used germ-free mice. Germ-free mice differ from conventional mice in that first, they do not normally develop colitis, even in the absence of IL-10 (Eaton et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eaton et al., 2011.

claim: Il10-/- mice that are housed in the presence of enteric microbes develop varying levels of colitis that appear to depend on their specific microbiota.
source: Il10-/- mice that are housed in the presence of enteric microbes develop varying levels of colitis that appear to depend on their specific microbiota.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Il10-/- mice.

claim: Germ-free mice differ from specific-pathogen-free (SPF) mice in their hepatic metabolism.
source: Also, germ-free mice differ from specific-pathogen-free (SPF) mice in their hepatic metabolism. Because AOM is a hepatotoxin in addition to a carcinogen, its toxicity may be altered in mice without a normal microbiota (Selwyn et al., 2016; Tung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Selwyn et al., 2016 and Tung et al., 2017.

claim: Because AOM is a hepatotoxin in addition to a carcinogen, its toxicity may be altered in mice without a normal microbiota.
source: Also, germ-free mice differ from specific-pathogen-free (SPF) mice in their hepatic metabolism. Because AOM is a hepatotoxin in addition to a carcinogen, its toxicity may be altered in mice without a normal microbiota (Selwyn et al., 2016; Tung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Selwyn et al., 2016 and Tung et al., 2017.

claim: Mouse strains differ in their response to AOM with the effect also modulated by non-genetic factors, like diet, which tend to vary widely across studies making it difficult to directly compare results.
source: Mouse strains differ in their response to AOM with the effect also modulated by non-genetic factors, like diet, which tend to vary widely across studies making it difficult to directly compare results (Bissahoyo et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bissahoyo et al., 2005.

claim: The dose and protocol of AOM used were below the published toxic dose for AOM in mice.
source: AOM is a known hepatoxin, but the dose and protocol used were below the published toxic dose for AOM in mice (Bissahoyo et al., 2005), and were not expected to cause lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bissahoyo et al., 2005.

claim: The AOM dose and protocol used were not expected to cause liver lesions.
source: AOM is a known hepatoxin, but the dose and protocol used were below the published toxic dose for AOM in mice (Bissahoyo et al., 2005), and were not expected to cause lesions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the dose being below the toxic threshold.
